title: Get lost in Kaleiçi, end at the old harbor
tagline: Ottoman houses, Roman walls and bougainvillea lanes sloping down to a tiny crescent harbor cut into the cliffs.
when: morning or golden hour — skip midday in summer
why: Kaleiçi is the walled old town Antalya grew out of — Roman, Byzantine, Seljuk and Ottoman layers stacked on the same few streets, with the fluted Yivli Minare rising over it all and the lanes running downhill to a small harbor tucked into a notch in the cliffs. Unlike a museum quarter, people still live here: laundry over courtyards, cats on doorsteps, a mosque that spent centuries as a church. It's the fastest way to understand that Antalya is an ancient port city first and a resort second.
take: Go early or at golden hour and get lost on purpose — the main lanes near the harbor are souvenir territory, and the quiet back streets a block away are where Kaleiçi actually wins. Walk in through Hadrian's Gate, drift downhill, and finish with a çay overlooking the harbor. In July and August treat it strictly as a morning or evening place; the lanes hold the heat. This is our default first walk with every newcomer.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: Yivli Minare — the fluted Seljuk minaret that is the city's symbol.
Kesik Minare (the 'broken minaret') — a Roman temple turned church turned mosque, the whole city's history in one building.
Hıdırlık Tower at the seaward corner, where the walls meet the cliff edge.
The harbor viewpoint from the walls above — better than the quay itself.

title: Sunset from Karaalioğlu Park
tagline: Tea at the cliff edge, the whole gulf below, and the Beydağları mountains turning purple across the water.
why: Central Antalya sits on top of sea cliffs, and Karaalioğlu Park is the long green balcony where the city takes that in: benches and tea gardens right on the edge, the Mediterranean below, and the wall of the Beydağları range rising across the gulf. The sun goes down behind those mountains, not into a flat sea horizon, and the light show on the peaks is better for it. This is where you learn Antalya's real backdrop is vertical.
take: Order a çay, claim a cliff-edge bench, and stay through the last light — it works in January as well as June, and in high summer it's the hour the city finally exhales. Hıdırlık Tower is at the park's Kaleiçi end, so it chains perfectly onto an old-town evening. Costs nothing, and it's the first place we take visitors who think Antalya is only hotels and beaches.

title: Evenings on the Konyaaltı promenade
tagline: A long pebble beach with mountains rising straight out of the sea — and the city's after-work swim ritual.
why: Konyaaltı is the beach Antalya actually uses: kilometres of pebble shore and a redesigned promenade running west from the cliffs, with the Beydağları standing straight up out of the sea ahead of you. On summer evenings half the city is here — swimming after work, walking, picnicking on the grass strips. The difference between living in Antalya and visiting is exactly this: the sea stops being an excursion and becomes part of the daily routine.
take: Come at the end of the day, not the middle — the evening swim-and-walk is the local rhythm, and the water stays swimmable far longer into autumn than you'd expect. It's pebbles, not sand, so swim shoes save your feet. The western stretches toward Liman and Hurma are calmer than the Beach Park end. Do this once and you'll understand why people move here.

title: Walk through Hadrian's Gate
tagline: A Roman triple arch from the 130s AD, still the front door between the modern city and the old town.
when: any time — lit up at night
why: Built for the emperor Hadrian's visit nearly nineteen centuries ago, the three marble arches of Üçkapılar still stand in the old city walls on Atatürk Caddesi — and they're not roped off in a site somewhere, they're a working entrance. The old Roman road level sits below today's street, grooved by centuries of cart wheels, and you walk over it on your way into Kaleiçi. Few cities let you commute through antiquity.
take: Make it your default way into the old town rather than a destination of its own — through the gate, down into the lanes, done. Look down at the worn Roman roadway as you cross, and come past at night once, when the marble is lit. It's a twenty-minute stop that quietly resets your sense of how old this city is.

title: The waterfall that falls into the sea
tagline: At the Lara cliffs, the Düden river simply leaps off the edge into the Mediterranean.
why: The Lower Düden waterfall is one of the strangest, best free sights in Turkey: a full river reaches the edge of the Lara cliffs and drops straight into the open sea, spray drifting over the water. The cliff-top park beside it is a classic local picnic and tea spot, and the plume is visible from boats out on the gulf. Ten minutes from the Lara beach neighborhoods, and most tourists never learn it exists.
take: See it twice: once from the cliff-top park at golden hour with a çay, and once from the water — the harbor excursion boats from Kaleiçi pass right under it, and from sea level it's genuinely dramatic. Pair the park visit with an evening on Lara's beach side. The flow varies with the season, but the cliff-edge setting never disappoints.

title: Upper Düden: walk behind the waterfall
tagline: A shaded park in Kepez where a path leads into the cave behind the falling water.
when: a hot afternoon — the spray is the point
why: Before the Düden river makes its famous leap into the sea, it surfaces at Düdenbaşı in Kepez and pours over a travertine ledge into a green, shaded gorge — and a path lets you walk into the cave behind the curtain of water. The park around it is one of the coolest places in the city on a hot day, in the literal sense: spray, shade, and the roar of water while the rest of Antalya bakes.
take: Save this one for the brutal months — in July and August it's the city's natural air conditioning, and going behind the falls is the kind of small adventure that makes a weekday evening feel like a trip. Expect local families and picnics rather than a wilderness experience; that's part of its charm. Easy to reach from the center without a car.

title: The Antalya Museum
tagline: One of Turkey's great archaeology museums — the gods of Perge, imperial statues and sarcophagi, most of it dug up nearby.
why: This coast was Pamphylia and Lycia, and the Antalya Museum holds what the region's ancient cities gave up: hall after hall of Roman statuary from Perge — emperors, gods and dancers — plus carved sarcophagi, prehistoric finds from local caves, and the ethnography of the Yörük nomads who summered in these mountains within living memory. It turns every ruin you'll visit afterwards from rubble into a story.
take: Go before you do the ancient-city day trips, not after — once you've stood in front of the Perge gallery, the empty colonnades out on the coast repopulate themselves in your head. It's air-conditioned, which makes it the honest answer to 'what do I do in Antalya in August at 3pm'. The walk along the cliff road makes getting there half the outing.

title: A weekly pazar morning
tagline: Antalya grows half of what Turkey eats — buy it at your neighborhood's weekly market, gözleme included.
when: your neighborhood's market day, in the morning
why: Antalya's coastal plain is Turkey's market garden — the greenhouses you pass on every drive supply the whole country — and the weekly neighborhood pazars are where that abundance lands, hours from the field. Every district has its day: rotating markets of produce, olives, cheese, herbs and household everything, with gözleme griddles going at the edges. Shopping at yours is one of the fastest ways to stop being a stranger where you live.
take: Ask a neighbor or your building's WhatsApp group which day your pazar sets up — everyone knows, and asking is itself a good icebreaker. Go in the morning with a trolley or big bags, buy what looks best rather than what you planned, and eat a gözleme standing up. Prices and quality both beat the supermarket, and stallholders start recognizing you by the third week. That feeling is the point.

title: Piyaz, hibeş and şiş köfte: eat like Antalya
tagline: The city's own table — tahini-drenched white beans, a cumin-tahini dip, and grilled köfte in old-school lokantas.
why: Antalya has its own food identity, and it isn't hotel buffets. Piyaz here means something it means nowhere else in Turkey: white beans dressed in a thick tahini sauce, served as a dish in its own right, not a side salad. Alongside it come hibeş — a fiery tahini-and-cumin dip scooped up with bread — and şiş köfte off the grill. The old köfte-piyaz lokantas that serve this trio are where working Antalya actually eats lunch.
take: Order piyaz as a main, not a garnish — that's the local way and the whole revelation. The right venue is a plain, busy lokanta with a queue at noon; follow the crowd, not the decor. This meal is cheap, fast and completely of this city, and doing it in your first week beats any restaurant list we could write. Doing it weekly is how you start to belong.

title: Kaleiçi after dark
tagline: Courtyard bars in Ottoman houses, rooftops over the harbor, and lanes that stay warm past midnight.
why: At night the old town changes character: the day-trip crowds drain away and Kaleiçi's real nightlife surfaces — bars in the courtyards of restored Ottoman houses, rooftop terraces looking over the harbor and the dark gulf, live music drifting out of the lanes. In an Antalya summer the evening is when the city properly wakes up, and Kaleiçi is the most walkable, most atmospheric place to spend it.
take: Skip the harbor-front strip, which mostly performs for tourists, and head for the courtyard and rooftop places in the back lanes — a garden under orange trees beats a laminated menu with photos every time. Summer nights run late because they finally can; ten o'clock is early. It's an easy district to go out in solo or in a small group, which is why our Antalya evenings will keep landing here.

title: Termessos, the eagle's nest
tagline: A mountain city even Alexander the Great gave up on — its theatre perched over a gorge, reclaimed by pines.
time: half a day with the drive
when: a clear day, autumn to spring
why: High in the mountains behind the city, inside a national park in Döşemealtı, Termessos is the ruin that ruins other ruins for you. The Pisidians built their city so high and so defensible that Alexander the Great looked at it and moved on. Because it was never rebuilt below, everything is still up there among the pines — and the theatre, on the edge of a gorge with mountains beyond, has a fair claim to the most dramatic setting of any ancient site in Turkey. You'll often have it nearly to yourself.
take: This is a proper walk, not a stroll — a steep uphill path from the car park in real mountain terrain, so wear actual shoes and carry water. We'd firmly point you at autumn through spring: the altitude softens the heat but the climb in July is still punishing, and on a clear winter day it's magnificent. You need a car (or a shared one — good small-group Smileys outing). Sit in the top rows of the theatre and let it go quiet.

title: Swim at Phaselis, on the Kemer coast
tagline: A ruined Lycian harbor city in a pine forest — with three bays you can actually swim in.
when: early on a summer morning, or any warm shoulder-season day
why: Down the coast past Kemer, Phaselis is the day trip that feels illegal: an ancient trading city on a pine-covered peninsula, its aqueduct and colonnaded street running between three bays — and you're allowed to swim in them. Shade from the pines, ruins at the waterline, mountains behind. It's the distilled promise of this coast: antiquity and the sea in the same hour, under an hour from the city.
take: In high summer go early — tour boats arrive late morning and the magic thins — or better, go on a warm May or October day when the water's still good and the bays are quiet. Bring everything: it's a protected site among trees, not a beach club, which is exactly why we love it. Swimming off a two-thousand-year-old harbor mole does not get old. Kemer town works for a late lunch on the way back.

title: Olympos, Çıralı and the eternal flames
tagline: Ruins in a jungle valley, a long protected beach, and hillside vents that have burned for thousands of years.
when: a warm weekend; the flames after dark
why: An hour and a half down the coast, the ruins of ancient Olympos lie tangled in greenery along a river valley that opens onto the sea, sharing a long, wild beach with the village of Çıralı — protected as a loggerhead-turtle nesting shore, so it has stayed blissfully unbuilt. On the hillside above burns the Chimaera: natural gas seeping from the rock and flaming day and night, as it has since antiquity, when it was a sea mark and a legend. Nowhere else near Antalya packs this much strangeness into one valley.
take: Do it overnight if you possibly can — a pansiyon in Çıralı or one of Olympos's famous rustic camps — because the Chimaera is an after-dark experience: a steady uphill walk by flashlight, then flames flickering out of bare rock under the stars. Days go to the beach and the overgrown ruins. This is the coast at its least commercial and the single trip our members will talk about most; spring and autumn are the sweet spots.

title: Side: the temples on the harbor
tagline: Marble columns of Apollo's temple at the tip of the old harbor — best at sunset, best off-season.
time: half a day with the drive
why: East along the coast, the modern resort town of Side sits literally inside the ancient one: a colonnaded Roman street runs through the middle of town, a huge theatre looms over the shops, and out at the harbor tip the re-erected columns of the Temple of Apollo stand against open sea. At sunset, with the light going gold behind the marble, it's one of the classic images of this whole coast — and the ruins themselves are free to wander into.
take: Time it for late afternoon so you're at the temple as the sun drops — that half hour is the reason to come. We'll be honest about the rest: in high summer the town is a full-volume resort, so either embrace that or do what we prefer and come off-season, when the colonnaded street empties out and the place breathes. Pairs into one long day with a slow fish dinner by the old harbor before the drive back.
